rationale:
Evidence: iteration 3 (score 396.3) is the best design so far. Its oval finish rate is 100% at 1.70 s mean, so the sensor layout and turn response work on gentle curves. Iteration 4 raised kp to 5.5, kd to 1.0 and cut base_speed to 1.05. That lifted s-bend progress (0.46 to 0.61) but dropped oval finish rate to 65% and the score to 356, so the gain/speed change traded oval reliability for bend progress. Iteration 1 to 3 also shows that a narrower wheel track (0.12 to 0.10) with kp 5 and kd 0.8 raised oval completion from 0.65 to 1.0. Slalom still fails at progress 0.09 to 0.15 with max_error about 0.062, just above the 0.06 m limit, and body width is already at its maximum, so the fix has to come from turning authority or control. Steering oscillation and RMS error stay small, so the robot is not ringing; it is pushed outward on sharp bends.

Changes, all from iteration 3 except the controller gains are unchanged: (1) wheel_track 0.10 to 0.09 m, a further ~11% increase in yaw per unit of turn command, continuing the trend that helped iterations 1 to 3. (2) mass 0.6 to 0.5 kg, which lowers yaw inertia so the robot turns faster for the same wheel command. (3) kp 5.0, ki 0.2, kd 0.8 and base_speed 1.2 kept, so iteration 4's gain/speed change is not repeated and the effect of the geometry change is isolated. Sensor layout (12 mm, x = -0.03 to +0.03, y = 0.05) is unchanged.

Expected result: s-bend and slalom progress rise (target s-bend above 0.6, slalom above 0.25), line_loss_events fall below 1 on those tracks, and oval completion holds at or near 1.0 with completion time around 1.7 s. Hypotheses: (H1) the faster yaw response from the narrower track and lighter robot is the main driver of better bend tracking; (H2) if oval completion drops, the extra yaw authority is causing overshoot, and kd should rise to about 0.9 rather than kp being cut. Measurements next: per-track completion, progress, max_error against 0.06, line_loss_events, steering_oscillation, and oval completion_time.
